(The Frisky) -- When I once asked an old friend why she hadn't simply ended things with her live-in boyfriend before embarking on a tangled affair with a married neighbor, she retorted sharply, "Don't be naive—no one leaves a relationship without already having another one lined up." Such individuals—call them "Overlappers"—refuse to end one relationship until the next is firmly in place. I balked at this notion, insisting that people do walk away from relationships without a safety net all the time, often driven by heartbreak or anger. Yet, reflecting on her history, I realized she had never once done so. Even when she plainly despised the man she was with, she remained until his successor was secured. I could never quite understand why. My friend is beautiful, accomplished, and remarkably intelligent; surely a brief stint of being single wouldn't be the end of the world for her.

Women, of course, are not alone in this tendency. I have known—and regrettably dated—no shortage of men who glide from one relationship directly into the next, often with considerable overlap, entangling the two like some murky Venn diagram. I understand that being single can, at times, feel lonely or tedious, but there are compelling reasons to avoid becoming—or dating—an Overlapper.

1. **Karma.** While overlapping relationships certainly constitutes a form of infidelity, what sets Overlappers apart is their calculated intent: they enter one relationship expressly to ease the transition into another. Regardless of how it's framed, this behavior involves deceiving one or both parties to serve their own ends. Relationships built on such dishonesty tend to exact a price eventually. At the very least, you can never fully trust an Overlapper—for, as another well-worn but accurate saying goes, if he did it with you, he'll do it to you.

2. **Drama.** Breakups are rarely pleasant, but those precipitated by infidelity are, without question, the most volatile. If your situation mirrors that of my friend and her partner (who, against considerable odds, did leave his wife), your nights as a "new couple" won't be filled with romance and butterflies, but rather with strategizing over hidden assets and debating whether your costly attorney is cutthroat enough. Hardly the stuff of fairy tales.

3. **The Pressure.** Though they may seem self-sufficient, individuals incapable of being alone often crave validation—the need to see themselves reflected favorably in another's admiring gaze. The moment that mirror (their partner) reveals an imperfection—be it weight gain, a career setback, or otherwise—their own self-image falters in turn. As natural narcissists, they demand nothing short of perfection, prompting them to seek out a new reflection. So take note: if you wish to hold onto an Overlapper, you'd best remain at your absolute best.

4. **Hardly a Charming Tale.** "I met my boyfriend when his puppy peed on my foot" makes for an ideal meet-cute story—it has chance, humor, and an adorable puppy to boot. # The Overlapper Phenomenon: When Relationship Transitions Become Deception

In the landscape of modern relationships, there exists a particular pattern of behavior worth examining closely—one embodied by individuals we might call "Overlappers." These are people who cannot bring themselves to end a current relationship until they have already lined up its replacement. Rather than experiencing the discomfort of being single, even temporarily, they engineer a seamless transition from one partner to the next, ensuring there's never a gap in their romantic life.

## Not a Gendered Behavior

It would be a mistake to assume this pattern belongs to one gender more than another. While stereotypes might suggest otherwise, the reality is that men engage in this behavior just as frequently as women do. Plenty of men maintain one relationship right up until the moment a new one is secured, moving from partner to partner with substantial overlap in between. This is a human behavioral pattern, not a gendered one, and recognizing this helps us understand it more clearly without falling into biased assumptions about who is "more likely" to cheat or manipulate.

## The Dishonesty at the Core

At its heart, overlapping is a form of dishonesty—and more specifically, it's cheating. Whether the Overlapper is deceiving their current partner (who believes the relationship is intact and exclusive), their future partner (who may not realize they're being used as an escape hatch), or both simultaneously, the common thread is manipulation. These individuals aren't being upfront about their intentions or actions; instead, they're orchestrating their romantic lives to serve their own emotional needs and comfort, often at the expense of the people who trust them.

## The Trust Problem You Inherit

If you find yourself becoming involved with an Overlapper—perhaps even becoming the "new" relationship they transitioned into—it's worth pausing to consider what this means for your own relationship's foundation. The logic here is straightforward but important: someone who was willing to cheat and deceive in order to be with you has already demonstrated their capacity for that kind of behavior. This doesn't guarantee they will cheat while in a relationship with you, but it does raise a legitimate concern. A person's past behavior, especially behavior exhibited in the very process that led to your relationship, often serves as a meaningful indicator of future conduct.

## Born from Chaos, Not Romance

Perhaps one of the most telling signs of an Overlapper relationship is how it begins. Rather than starting with the typical excitement, nervousness, and gradual building of trust that characterizes most new romantic beginnings, these relationships frequently launch amid drama, tension, and explosive conflict. There are confrontations, confessions, and the fallout from broken relationships to contend with right from the outset. Instead of a clean slate, the relationship inherits the wreckage of infidelity—setting a precedent for how conflict, trust, and communication will be handled moving forward. A relationship born in chaos often struggles to find the stable, honest footing that healthy partnerships require.

# The Overlappers: When Fear of Being Alone Leads to Deception

There's a particular type of person moving through the dating world who never seems to be single. One relationship ends, and almost immediately—sometimes even before it officially ends—another begins. They're rarely, if ever, alone. Let's call them "Overlappers."

At first glance, this pattern might seem like nothing more than a string of romantic good fortune, or perhaps evidence of an especially charming and desirable personality. But look closer, and a more troubling dynamic often emerges. Overlappers frequently engage in a kind of quiet, corrosive deception: they begin securing their next relationship *before* ending their current one. They flirt, they connect, they build emotional (and sometimes physical) intimacy with a new person, all while their current partner remains unaware that the relationship is already, in effect, over.

## The Mechanics of Overlapping

The pattern usually unfolds in a predictable way. As a current relationship becomes difficult, unsatisfying, or simply stale, the Overlapper doesn't do the hard work of ending it, sitting with the discomfort, and figuring out what they actually want. Instead, they start looking outward. A new connection forms—maybe through work, a mutual friend, a dating app "just to see what's out there," or an old flame resurfacing at a convenient moment.

This new connection becomes a kind of insurance policy. It provides emotional validation, excitement, and the reassurance that they are still desirable, all while their current partner is left in the dark. Only once the new relationship feels secure—once the Overlapper is confident they have a soft place to land—do they finally end things with their current partner.

## Why They Do It: The Fear Beneath the Behavior

At the root of this pattern lies a deep and often unexamined fear: the fear of being alone. For the Overlapper, singleness isn't experienced as a neutral or potentially valuable state—it's experienced as a kind of existential threat. Being without a partner might mean confronting difficult questions: *Am I lovable on my own? What do I actually want from a relationship? What role did I play in this relationship's failure?*

Rather than face these questions, the Overlapper sidesteps them entirely. By ensuring there's always someone waiting in the wings, they never have to experience the discomfort of solitude, the anxiety of not knowing what comes next, or the vulnerability of self-reflection. The presence of a new partner numbs the pain of loss and short-circuits any real reckoning with what went wrong.

## Why This Pattern Matters

This behavior isn't just a minor character flaw or a harmless quirk of modern dating—it has real and often devastating consequences.

**It systematically undermines trust.** The partner being left behind is deceived, often for weeks or months, about the true state of the relationship. They may sense something is wrong, but are frequently reassured, gaslit, or simply kept in the dark. When the truth eventually surfaces, it can feel like a fundamental betrayal, not just of fidelity, but of the entire relationship's authenticity.

**It creates unnecessarily dramatic and painful endings.** Because the new relationship typically involves some form of infidelity (whether emotional or physical), the breakup that follows is rarely clean. Instead, it becomes tangled up in accusations, revelations of betrayal, and the added pain of comparison—being replaced feels different, and often worse, than simply being left. The betrayed partner is forced to grapple not only with the end of the relationship but with the humiliation of having been deceived.

**It robs the Overlapper of critical self-knowledge.** Perhaps most significantly, this pattern prevents Overlappers themselves from growing. The period between relationships—often uncomfortable, sometimes lonely—is also where crucial self-reflection happens. It's where people can examine their patterns, understand their contributions to past relationship failures, and develop a stronger sense of who they are independent of a partner. By never allowing themselves this space, Overlappers remain stuck in a cycle: entering new relationships not from a place of genuine readiness and self-understanding, but from unresolved fear and unexamined habits. This often means they carry the same unaddressed issues from one relationship to the next, setting up future relationships to fail in similar ways.

## Breaking the Cycle

Recognizing this pattern—whether in oneself or in a partner—is the first step toward change. For Overlappers, the challenge lies in learning to tolerate the discomfort of being alone, to see solitude not as a void to be filled but as an opportunity for genuine growth. For those who suspect they're involved with an Overlapper, understanding this dynamic can offer clarity: the dishonesty isn't necessarily a reflection of their own worth, but rather a symptom of the other person's unresolved fear of solitude.

Ultimately, breaking this pattern requires a willingness to sit with uncertainty, to face the anxiety of not knowing what comes next, and to trust that one's own company—however briefly—is not something to be feared, but something worth getting to know.

# The Frisky

There was once a small sailboat named *The Frisky*, moored at the edge of a quiet harbor town. She wasn't the fastest vessel in the marina, nor the most elegant, but she had a certain charm—chipped blue paint, a slightly crooked mast, and a name that made people smile when they read it on her hull.

*The Frisky* belonged to an old fisherman named Walt, who had inherited her from his father decades ago. Every morning, when the fog still clung to the water and the gulls had just begun their restless cries, Walt would untie her ropes and guide her out past the breakwater.

When the wind was kind, *The Frisky* danced across the waves like she was living up to her name—leaping over swells, tilting playfully with each gust, as if she remembered being young. When the sea was calm, she drifted lazily, content to let the current carry her wherever it pleased.

The townspeople grew fond of watching her return each evening, her sails catching the last orange light of sunset. Children would run to the dock when they heard Walt's whistle, eager to hear stories about the fish he'd caught or the storms he'd weathered.

Years passed, and Walt grew older, his hands more weathered than the boat's timbers. But *The Frisky* remained steady—not because she never changed, but because she was cared for, patched up, and loved through every season.

When Walt finally passed, it was his granddaughter who took the helm. She didn't know much about sailing at first, but she learned quickly, guided by the boat's familiar creaks and the memory of her grandfather's laughter.

*The Frisky* still sails today, a little more weathered, a little more storied—but frisky still, especially when the wind picks up just right.

# The Serial Monogamist's Dirty Secret: Why "Never Single" Isn't Romantic, It's a Warning Label

Let's talk about that person. You know the one. They've had a partner attached to their hip since approximately their sophomore year of high school, cycling through relationships like they're returning items at Zara—never once experiencing that awkward, formative period of just... being alone with themselves.

We've been conditioned to see this as relationship prowess. "Wow, they're just so lovable!" Cute story, but also: red flag the size of a parade float.

**Here's the uncomfortable truth:** if someone hasn't spent meaningful time single, they don't actually know how to be *with* someone—they only know how to avoid being *without* someone. There's a difference, and it's the difference between intimacy and terror management.

## The Relationship-as-Life-Support System

People who chain-date are often using partners as a psychological safety net rather than choosing them as, you know, a person they're into. This means you're not being selected for who you are. You're being selected because you happen to be standing there when the previous relationship ended and the panic set in.

Romantic, right?

## They Never Learned to Sit With Themselves

Being single—really single, not "single for two weeks between situationships" single—forces you to develop an actual relationship with yourself. You figure out what you want versus what you'll settle for. You get bored, and you learn that boredom won't kill you. You cry alone in your apartment and realize the apartment is still standing afterward.

Skip that step, and you've got someone who has literally no idea who they are outside the context of a partnership. Which means when you two hit inevitable rough patches, they won't have the internal resources to self-soothe. You become the resource. Forever. Exhausting!

## The Breakup Timeline Should Scare You

If someone's last relationship ended eight days before yours began, ask yourself: did they process that relationship, or did they just relocate the trauma into your DMs? Grief and reflection take time. Skipping straight to a new relationship isn't resilience—it's avoidance wearing a cute outfit.

## What This Means for You, Specifically

You will likely become a rebound whether you're the fourth person or the fourteenth, because the *pattern itself* is the problem, not any particular ex. You're not dating a person who chose singleness as valid and then chose you. You're dating someone terrified of an empty Tuesday night.

**The fix isn't complicated, but it does require patience:** if you're interested in a serial monogamist, encourage (or honestly, wait for) an actual stretch of solo time before you get serious. If they can't tolerate being alone long enough to reflect, they're not ready to be *with* someone—they're just ready to not be alone.

There's a difference. Insist on it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

# 4 Reasons Not to Date an "Overlapper"

My friend Rachel (name changed, obviously) once told me about the time she got involved with a married man who lived two doors down from her. It didn't start as an affair, at least not in his mind. "He told me things were basically over with his wife," she said. "They just hadn't figured out the logistics yet." Six months later, he was still living with his wife, still sleeping in the same bed, and still texting Rachel goodnight from the bathroom with the fan running so no one would hear him.

When his wife eventually found out, he didn't leave. He apologized to her, deleted his second phone, and Rachel never heard from him again.

What Rachel dated wasn't a man in a bad marriage. She dated an *overlapper*—someone who moves from one relationship into the next without ever actually being single in between. And if you've ever been tempted to be the "next chapter" for someone who hasn't finished writing the last one, here's why you should close that book and walk away.

## 1. You're Not a New Beginning—You're an Exit Strategy

Overlappers rarely leave a relationship because they've found clarity. They leave because they found a replacement. That distinction matters enormously. It means the decision to end things wasn't made on its own merits—it was outsourced to you. You didn't get chosen; you got *used* as leverage to make an already-crumbling situation collapse faster. That's not romantic. That's logistics.

## 2. If They'll Do It To Someone Else, They'll Do It To You

The math here is simple and unforgiving: the same person who justified deceiving their partner to be with you will one day need an equally convincing justification to deceive *you*. Cheating isn't a one-time moral lapse for an overlapper—it's a coping mechanism. They don't know how to end things cleanly, so they build an escape hatch before they need one. Rachel wasn't an anomaly in that man's life. She was a pattern.

## 3. You Never Get an Honest Beginning

Every relationship needs an origin story you can look back on without flinching. Overlappers rob you of that. Instead of "we met and fell for each other," your story becomes "we met while he was still legally, practically, emotionally tangled up with someone else." That means secrecy, guilt, and shame get baked into the foundation before you've even had a first real date. You'll spend the relationship trying to build trust on ground that was never solid to begin with.

## 4. You Become the Villain in Someone Else's Story

Even if you didn't know about the wife, the girlfriend, or the situation—even if you were genuinely deceived—you still end up cast as "the other person" in someone else's narrative. That's not fair, but it's real. Rachel spent months being quietly, unfairly hated by a woman she never met, for a decision she didn't fully understand she was part of. Overlappers don't just hurt their partners. They recruit unwitting accomplices.

---

The tell, in hindsight, is almost always obvious: overlappers talk about their current relationship in the past tense while it's still very much in the present. "We're basically done." "It's over, we're just waiting for the right time." "She knows things aren't working." If someone is telling you the ending of a story that hasn't ended yet, believe the present, not the narration.

Because the real red flag was never the marriage next door. It was that he was already halfway out the door of one relationship while stepping through the door of another—without ever actually closing the first one behind him.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

# Confessions of a Serial Monogamist Detective (Or: How I Learned to Spot the Overlappers)

Let's talk about a very specific breed of ex: the Overlapper. You know the type. The one who never—and I mean *never*—experiences even a fleeting moment of singlehood, because that would require sitting with themselves, and God forbid.

I've dated three of them. THREE. At this point I should get a punch card.

Here's how it works: They're "not happy" in their relationship for months, sometimes years, before they ever mention it to you. They're just quietly interviewing your replacement while still sleeping next to you, still saying "I love you," still using your Netflix password. Then one day, seemingly out of nowhere, they're "falling out of love" and it's "been coming for a while" and—plot twist—they've already got someone lined up. Someone who, weirdly, they've been texting "as friends" for the last four months. Someone who definitely isn't the reason things ended, they'll insist, eyes darting like a raccoon caught in a trash can.

Sure, Jan.

## The Overlapper's Greatest Hits

**"We were basically already broken up."** According to who? You? Did you get a memo? Because I distinctly remember making dinner reservations for our anniversary three weeks before this "inevitable" split.

**"I didn't want to be alone."** Groundbreaking. Truly no one has ever felt this before. Most of us just, you know, deal with it. With ice cream and bad decisions and re-watching the same six episodes of *Friends*. We don't preemptively install a new person like a backup generator.

**"It just happened."** Nothing "just happens" over a four-month emotional affair, Kevin. That's not spontaneous combustion, that's a *slow burn you personally tended.*

## Why They Do It

Look, I get the ick factor of being alone. Solitude is uncomfortable! It forces you to reckon with why your last relationship failed instead of sprinting toward a shiny new person who thinks your jokes are still funny and hasn't yet discovered you leave cabinet doors open like a feral raccoon.

But here's the thing about Overlappers: they're not actually avoiding loneliness. They're avoiding *accountability.* Because if there's always a next person ready to catch them, they never have to fall. They never have to ask why they keep ending up unhappy. They just keep changing the cast while the plot stays exactly the same.

## What I've Learned (The Hard Way, Obviously)

If someone can't tell you they're unhappy *before* they've got an understudy waiting in the wings, that's not romantic fate, that's cowardice with really good timing. 

The red flags are always there in retrospect: the sudden "work friend," the phone that's face-down now, the way they stopped fighting for the relationship right around the time someone new started liking their Instagram stories a little too enthusiastically.

So here's my unsolicited advice: if you're dating someone who's never been single, not even for a hot minute, ask yourself why. And if you catch your partner overlapping *you* into their next chapter? Don't stick around to read the footnotes. 

Let them go be someone else's emotional life raft. You deserve someone who can actually swim.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

# 7 Reasons Dating a Serial Monogamist Is a Trap You Don't Want to Fall Into

We all know one. The person who has never—not once—been single for longer than a Taylor Swift breakup song. They slide from relationship to relationship like it's a game of hopscotch, barely touching the ground of solitude before landing in someone else's arms. Tempting as it may be to think *"this time it's different,"* here's why dating the serial monogamist might leave you starring in your own cautionary tale.

**1. Karma**
If they left their last five partners in the emotional dust to immediately date someone new, guess what? You're now "someone new" to their *next* someone new. What goes around, comes around—and it comes around fast with these people.

**2. Drama**
Where there's a string of relationships, there's a string of exes, unresolved feelings, and group chats you were never meant to see. Buckle up.

**3. The Pressure**
They don't know how to just *vibe*. Three weeks in, they're already asking about meeting your parents. Why? Because they've never had to sit in the discomfort of not having a plan. You become the plan—fast.

**4. Not Cute**
Watching someone perform "healed and ready" behavior after a breakup that happened *ten days ago* is not the romantic reset they think it is. It's a red flag with a bow on it.

**5. The Rebound Rodeo**
Statistically speaking, you might just be a layover, not a destination. Serial monogamists often skip the self-reflection step, meaning you could be dating someone else's unresolved trauma wearing your name.

**6. Zero Self-Awareness**
Ask them why their last relationship ended and watch the mental gymnastics unfold. Spoiler: it's never their fault. Ever.

**7. You Become the Placeholder**
The scariest part? You might not even realize it until they're already onto the next one—because that's simply how they operate. Onward and upward, with or without you.

**Bottom line:** Loving someone who's never sat with themselves is like building a house on a foundation that's still under construction. Proceed with caution—or maybe just proceed elsewhere. 💅

# The Case for the Awkward Single Era (Or: Why You Should Try Sitting With Yourself Before Sitting Next to Someone New)

Okay, so we need to talk about serial monogamy's slightly unhinged cousin: the seamless transition. You know the one. Where someone's Instagram goes from "us" to "me" to a suspiciously well-lit "us" again within the span of about eleven days, and everyone in the group chat is pretending not to notice that the new partner looks remarkably like the old partner, just with better skin.

I'm not here to clutch pearls about people who move fast. Some people genuinely do meet the love of their life two weeks after a breakup. Sure. But let's talk about the other 90% of us, because I think we've collectively decided that being alone for even a hot minute is some kind of personal failure, and I would like to gently push back on that.

**The overlap problem**

Remember when Sarah — not her real name, but you know a Sarah — left her boyfriend of four years and was "casually seeing someone" within three weeks? She swore up and down it wasn't related to the breakup, that she'd "just met him at a work thing," and we all nodded along like supportive friends do. Fast forward eight months and she's texting at 1am about how the new guy has "some of the same issues" as the old guy, except now she also has zero perspective because she never actually processed leaving the first relationship. She just changed the scenery. The furniture in her emotional living room stayed exactly the same.

This is the thing about overlapping relationships, or the ones that start suspiciously close together — you're not actually ending anything. You're just adding a filter to the same photo.

**What actually happens when you sit in it**

I have a friend — genuinely one of the most emotionally solid people I know — who took fourteen months single after a divorce before dating again. Fourteen months! People thought she'd joined a cult of celibacy. But she said something that stuck with me: she needed to find out who she was when nobody was watching. Not performing "fine," not performing "healing," just actually being alone with her own thoughts on a random Tuesday night with nothing to distract her.

She figured out she'd been the "easy one" in every relationship since she was nineteen. The one who didn't rock the boat, who adjusted her personality like a thermostat depending on who she was with. It took months of actual solitude — not dating-app solitude, not situationship solitude, real solitude — to even notice that pattern, let alone interrupt it.

You cannot do that work while you're already halfway invested in someone new. The nervous system doesn't do "processing the last thing" and "auditioning for the next thing" simultaneously. It's like trying to do laundry while still wearing the dirty clothes.

**The "I don't want to be alone" trap**

Here's the uncomfortable part: a lot of quick rebounds aren't really about the new person. They're about not wanting to feel the specific, awful quiet of an empty apartment after someone's been in your space for years. That silence is genuinely brutal. I'm not being glib about it. But numbing that silence with a new person means you never actually learn that you can survive it. You just outsource the discomfort instead of building the muscle.

And the muscle matters, because eventually — in every relationship, even the healthy ones — there will be moments of loneliness *within* the relationship. If you've never sat with loneliness on your own, that moment inside a partnership can feel unbearable, like proof something's wrong, when really it's just... life. People who've done solo time tend to handle those moments with way less panic.

**Not a purity test**

To be clear, this isn't about some mandatory grief-widow period where you wear black and swear off flirting for a calendar year. It's not a moral failing to feel attraction quickly after a breakup. The issue isn't timeline, it's *substitution* — using someone new as scaffolding to avoid collapsing, instead of doing the collapsing (safely, with actual support) and rebuilding on your own foundation.

The single stretch is genuinely uncomfortable. It's supposed to be a little uncomfortable. That discomfort is information, not a problem to be solved by the next situationship. Give it some room before you hand the job to somebody else.
